items.followUp: State four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model places electrons in specific allowed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve in fixed orbits or occupy definite energy levels around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying fixed orbits or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in stationary orbits do not lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in a stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this stationary-orbit property.

rubric.why: An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy when it jumps to a higher orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the absorption and upward transition.

rubric.why: An electron emits energy to move to a lower orbit.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it jumps to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the emission and downward transition.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model allows only certain quantized values of electron angular momentum.
rubric.description: States that the electron’s angular momentum is quantized.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the quantization postulate.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
Electrons do not radiate energy while moving in a stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.

items.followUp: What is a covalent compound? State four of its properties.

rubric.why: An ionic compound consists of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic compound as a compound of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both high melting and high boiling points.

rubric.why: Hard crystalline form and solubility in water are characteristic textbook properties.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids and are generally soluble in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both properties are stated.

rubric.why: Ions are mobile and conduct electricity in the molten state or in aqueous solution.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for conductivity in either condition; do not award for claiming they conduct as solids.

modelAnswer: An ionic compound consists of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
They are hard crystalline solids and are generally soluble in water.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: What is a polyatomic ion? Give one example.

rubric.why: A radical is an atom or group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as a unit.
rubric.description: Defines a radical as a charged atom or group of atoms that behaves as a single unit.

rubric.why: Sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, and carbonate are valid examples of radicals.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a radical, such as sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, or carbonate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A radical is an atom or group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as a single unit in a chemical reaction.
For example, the sulfate radical is SO₄²⁻.

items.followUp: How many molecules are present in 0.5 mole of oxygen gas?

rubric.why: Avogadro’s number gives the number of particles in one mole.
rubric.description: Defines Avogadro’s number and gives its value as approximately 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the meaning and correct value.

rubric.why: The example applies the number to the atoms in one mole of carbon.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example with the correct number of particles, such as one mole of carbon containing 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example and particle count.

modelAnswer: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance: 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
For example, one mole of carbon contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
